solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Villain in novel underwear, liver coloured (4,4,6)

indicators.note: something coloured has been changed in appearance, so the letters of LIVER are altered

blocks.note: long johns are warm full-length underpants

explanation.surface: A lurid description of a fictional rogue: his underwear, his liver, his colouring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Villain in novel' reads like part of the surface, but it is the whole definition: the one-legged pirate of Treasure Island (which is also 28 across).
explanation.definitionFit: Long John Silver is the scheming pirate villain of Stevenson's Treasure Island.

clue.text: Maybe riding with son moving up from the sea (7)

definitions.note: onshore describes a wind or movement coming from the sea towards land

indicators.note: in a down clue, moving up means shifting a letter earlier in the word

blocks.note: riding is, for example, being ON HORSEback
HORSE with its S (son) moved up to the front

explanation.surface: Someone who has come in from the sea and gone riding with their son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe riding' is a definition by example: ON HORSE. Then the S for son climbs to the top of HORSE, turning it into SHORE.
explanation.definitionFit: An onshore breeze blows in from the sea towards the land.

clue.text: Fighter pleased a riot spread (9)

indicators.note: letters that are spread about are scattered into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A boxer delighted that a brawl has broken out and is spreading.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Fighter' a brawler cheering on a riot; the answer is the older, arena kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A gladiator was a trained fighter in the Roman arena.

clue.text: Bar in France where Whitman retired (6)

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so WALT is written backwards

explanation.surface: A French bar where the poet Walt Whitman spent his retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a place to drink in France, but it is a verb: to bar something is to outlaw it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to forbid by rule or law.

clue.text: New staff about to hold a card game (8)

indicators.note: the pieces hold A inside them

blocks.note: on = about, as in a talk on birds

explanation.surface: A new member of staff arriving to take charge of a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees and 'card game' as something the new hire must supervise, but staff here is a stick, and on means about as in a talk on birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon, or nap, is a trick-taking card game.

clue.text: Cool home some cool girls set up (5)

indicators.note: only some of the letters of 'cool girls' are used
in a down clue, set up means written upwards, so the letters are reversed

explanation.surface: Some trendy girls have set up home together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' does two jobs: literally cold in the definition, trendy in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is a home built of snow blocks, about as cool as a house gets.

clue.text: An artist’s shift I’m hesitant to interrupt (7)

indicators.note: ERM breaks into the middle of VEER

blocks.note: to veer is to shift direction
erm is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A hesitant painter trying to break into someone's work shift.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's means 'is', joining definition to wordplay; 'I'm hesitant' is the setter saying erm.
explanation.definitionFit: Johannes Vermeer was the Dutch painter of Girl with a Pearl Earring.

clue.text: Film city commander raving about nothing (8,6)

indicators.note: wild, frenzied talk, so the letters are jumbled
the jumbled letters go around O

explanation.surface: A town's military commander ranting about nothing in particular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film city' tempts you towards Hollywood or Bollywood, but 'Film' stands alone as the definition and 'city' starts the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the romcom is one genre of film.

clue.text: Sweet kid hurt his leg running back from cricket (7,7)

indicators.note: the letters run about into a new order
the back of cricket is its final letter

explanation.surface: A lovely child injured his leg while running between the wickets at cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like it describes the kid, but it is the definition. Turkish delight is a jelly confection dusted in sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: Turkish delight is a sweet made of flavoured jelly dusted with icing sugar.

clue.text: Arriviste jerk going on to Oxford (7)

indicators.note: something that goes on to another is added after it, so START follows UP

blocks.note: going up means going to university, especially Oxford or Cambridge
a start is a sudden jerk

explanation.surface: An ambitious social climber, a real jerk, heading off to Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' looks like an insult, fitting an arriviste, but it is a sudden movement. In British usage you go up to Oxford and come down when you leave.
explanation.definitionFit: An arriviste is a newcomer who has risen fast and is resented for it: an upstart.

clue.text: Traveller’s bundle, mostly depressing (7)

indicators.note: most of PILE, losing its final letter

blocks.note: a bundle of money is a pile; PILE without its last letter

explanation.surface: A backpacker's gloomy pack of belongings.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's means 'is'; 'bundle' is a large sum of money, a pile.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilgrim is a traveller making a journey to a holy place.

clue.text: Policy expert backed by one lofty US wise guy (4,2,3)

indicators.note: to back is to move backwards, so WONK runs in reverse

blocks.note: a policy wonk is a political expert

explanation.surface: A tall American smart alec supporting a government policy adviser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US' marks 'wise guy' as American slang for a smart alec, not the Mafia sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A know-it-all is someone who acts as if they know everything: a wise guy.

clue.text: Lines from Pindar performing classical theatre (5)

blocks.note: Pindar was the Greek poet famous for his odes

explanation.surface: An actor performing verses by Pindar in an ancient Greek theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: Odeon is now a British cinema chain, but the word first meant a roofed Greek or Roman building for music and recitals.
explanation.definitionFit: An odeon was a classical building for musical and poetic performances.

clue.text: When out at midday, lassies take sandwiches (6)

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer as a phrase; SIESTA is the noun for the midday rest when people are out

indicators.note: the words hold the answer between them like a sandwich filling

explanation.surface: Girls taking packed lunches out with them at noon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' reads as lunch, fitting 'midday', but it is a verb: the phrase sandwiches the answer. 'Out' means asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is the midday nap, when people are out cold.

clue.text: Note put on 100 formerly rare compositions (8)

indicators.note: TI is put on after the other pieces

blocks.note: R = rare, as on steak menus
ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A musician adding a note to a hundred once-rare works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' opens the clue but its letters come last: TI is put on the end of C, ONCE and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Concerti is the Italian plural of concerto, a musical composition.

clue.text: Friendly visit narrowly avoided disaster (5,4)

definitions.note: the definition is a verb phrase; CLOSE CALL is the noun for such an escape

blocks.note: to pay a call is to visit

explanation.surface: A social call that very nearly ended in catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one friendly visit gone wrong; the split falls after 'visit', and the rest is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the escape was so near the disaster that the call was close.

clue.text: Sort of clothing workers curse (8)

blocks.note: men = workers, as in the men on a building site

explanation.surface: Garment workers cursing the clothes they make.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workers curse' reads as a grumbling workforce; men for workers is an old crossword standby.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: menswear is one category of clothing, as a shop department would sort it.

clue.text: Act without role being set out (8)

indicators.note: in its old sense of outside: DEED goes outside PART

blocks.note: a part in a play is a role

explanation.surface: An actor performing with no part to play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' reads as lacking, but here it means outside, so the act wraps around the role.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: someone who has set out on a journey has left.

clue.text: Ward training nurses got ER prepared (7)

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so PE holds the rest
the letters of GOT ER are made ready in a new order

blocks.note: PE = physical education, school sports training

explanation.surface: A hospital ward where trainee nurses got the emergency room ready.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all hospitals: ward, nurses, ER. But 'Ward' is a person in someone's care, and 'nurses' means holds.
explanation.definitionFit: A protégé is someone under the care and guidance of a patron, like a ward.

clue.text: Magazine covers start off short of space (6)

indicators.note: to cover something is to lie around it, so COMIC wraps S
the start of short is its first letter

blocks.note: a comic is a magazine of strips

explanation.surface: A magazine's cover starts off by running short on space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short of space' looks like one phrase meaning cramped, but 'short' belongs to the wordplay and 'of space' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosmic means relating to the cosmos, of outer space.

clue.text: Bird’s bare bottom (one lacking tail parts) (7)

indicators.note: RHEA without its last letter
RHE parts MOON, splitting it open

blocks.note: to moon is to show your bare bottom
'one' is another bird, a RHEA, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A bird with a bald rump, missing some of its tail feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' points back to 'Bird', meaning another bird: the rhea, a big flightless South American bird. 'Tail parts' reads as feathers but is two instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: The moorhen is a common dark waterbird with a red bill.

clue.text: We hear this setter’s game for a cocktail (3,3)

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the answer sounds like the wordplay

blocks.note: this setter's = MY; a game or match, as in a cup tie = TIE

explanation.surface: A crossword setter describing their game as a way to earn a cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This setter's' is the setter speaking of themselves: MY. A tie is a knockout match, as in a cup tie.
explanation.definitionFit: A mai tai is a rum cocktail with lime and orgeat.

clue.text: Crazy place to go on vacation, Paraguay (5)

indicators.note: vacated, emptied of its middle, leaving the outside letters

blocks.note: a loo is a toilet, the place you go
PARAGUAY emptied, leaving P and Y

explanation.surface: An odd holiday destination: Paraguay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place to go on vacation' reads as a holiday spot, but it splits after 'go': the loo, then an emptied Paraguay.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial synonym: loopy suggests someone whose thinking has gone round in loops.

clue.text: A poet still penning a start to something (5)

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in, as sheep in a pen, so YET encloses A
the first letter of something

explanation.surface: A poet still writing the opening of a new piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' suits a poet, but here it means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: W B Yeats, the Irish Nobel laureate, is one poet among many.

clue.text: Position berth facing west in posh cabin (9)

indicators.note: in an across answer west is leftward, so MOOR is written backwards

blocks.note: to berth a ship is to moor it

explanation.surface: Choosing a berth on the west side of a luxury cabin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Berth' reads as a bunk, fitting a cabin, but it is a verb: to dock a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A stateroom is a private, well-appointed cabin on a ship.

clue.text: End of détente after island drops a bomb (7)

indicators.note: the final letter of détente
one thing placed after another follows it, so E comes behind the island
to drop something is to let it go, so GRENADA lets go of an A

blocks.note: GRENADA, the Caribbean island, without an A

explanation.surface: Détente ends when an island nation drops a bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a Cold War headline, and 'drops' seems to go with 'a bomb'; really it takes A off the island.
explanation.definitionFit: A grenade is a small hand-thrown bomb.

clue.text: Drunk badly beaten leaving hotel (7)

indicators.note: a guest leaving a hotel goes out of it; here H goes out of THRASHED

blocks.note: H = hotel in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A drunk, badly beaten up, stumbling out of a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a drunk thrown out of a hotel after a beating; 'hotel' is really just H, from the phonetic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang synonym: to be trashed is to be wrecked by drink.

clue.text: Book prize vacuous idiots win (8,6)

indicators.note: empty, so IDIOTS loses its middle and keeps I and S

blocks.note: to prize something is to treasure it
IDIOTS emptied, leaving I and S
to land a contract is to win it

explanation.surface: A literary prize won by empty-headed fools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book prize' reads as one phrase, like the Booker, but 'Book' is the definition and 'prize' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Treasure Island is Robert Louis Stevenson's pirate novel, home of 1 across.
